newsitem.title: USA: Judge OKs U.S. plan to restore Pacific salmon.
newsitem.headline: Judge OKs U.S. plan to restore Pacific salmon.

text.p: A federal judge has upheld the government's framework for managing the Columbia River system in a way intended to restore endangered salmon species.
U.S. District Judge Malcolm Marsh late Thursday rejected a challenge to the "biological opinion" by a coalition of environmental and recreational groups backed by tribal and state authorities.

In a 33-page order, Marsh said the opinion produced by the National Marine Fisheries Service met the requirements of the Endangered Species Act to restore salmon and other dwindling species in the Pacific Northwest.
But Marsh warned that "time is clearly running out" for many species that have been driven to the brink of extinction by dams and development.

Brian Gorman, spokesman for the fisheries service, said the ruling was "enormously" important and would allow the Bonneville Power Administration and Army Corps of Engineers to continue what he described as a four-year experiment involving water flows and salmon populations.

But Dan Rohlf, lead attorney for the environmental groups, said the Fisheries Service opinion made it difficult to achieve water flows sufficient to ensure salmon survival. He said even the government acknowledges that its plan only provides for a 50 percent chance that endangered salmon runs will survive to the middle of the next century.

"I find it quite troubling to think we are spending billions of dollars on a set of measures that at best have only a 50-50 chance of achieving their goal," he said. "At some level we need to decide whether we're serious about saving salmon or not."

Marsh said the fisheries service had provided a "reasoned evaluation" of factors affecting salmon survival, but he questioned whether the resulting framework for managing the river accepted too much risk.

"As a longtime observer and examiner of this process, I cannot help but question the soundness of the selected level of risk acceptance, but the (Endangered Species Act) says nothing about risk tolerance and the limits of judicial review dictate that I not interfere...," Marsh wrote.
Rohlf said the environmental groups would consider an appeal.
